prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso met with President Barack Obama on Tuesday making him the first head of state to be hosted by the new administration. Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso steps off his Boeing 747 at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland Monday. It was a long trip -- 6,800 miles (11,000 km) -- for a short meeting -- one hour -- and happened as Obama was preparing his first address to a joint session of Congress. Sitting next to Aso in the White House, Obama said: "The friendship between the United States and Japan is extraordinarily important. "It is for that reason that the prime minister is the first foreign dignitary to visit me in the Oval Office." Obama said the U.S.-Japanese alliance would be crucial in solving international problems including climate change. "We think we have to work together, not only on issues relating to the Pacific Rim, but throughout the world," Obama added. Aso said the global economy was also on the agenda at their meeting. "We are the number 1 and second biggest economies of the world. We will have to work hand in hand. "I think we are the only two nations which are powerful enough to solve those very critical, vital issue," Aso said. Japan's Cabinet Secretary Takeo Kawamura said that being the first to visit the Obama White House was an indication of the priority the new president placed on the relationship. Another topic likely to have been on the agenda was Japan's Asian neighbor North Korea, which U.S. intelligence says is preparing to test a long-range missile. Pyongyang has denied the charge, instead saying it is making preparations to launch a satellite. A test-fire by North Korea in 2006 failed 40 seconds after launch. The missile is thought to have an intended range of about 4,200 miles (6,700 kilometers), which -- if true -- could give it the capability of striking Alaska or Hawaii. Aso's visit to Washington comes, as his approval rating stands at a meager 11 percent, the second lowest ever recorded for a Japanese prime minister. Yoshiro Mori, a former prime minister, resigned after his rate bottomed out at 9 percent. Last week his finance minister Shoichi Nakagawa announced he will step down after coming under fire for appearing intoxicated at a weekend news conference during the G-7 meeting in Rome. CNN's Chie Kobayashi contributed to this report.

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso met with President Barack Obama on Tuesday, becoming the first head of state hosted by the new administration.

Aso stepped off his Boeing 747 at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland on Monday. It was a long journey—6,800 miles (11,000 kilometers)—for a brief, one-hour meeting, which took place as Obama prepared to deliver his first address to a joint session of Congress.

Sitting beside Aso at the White House, Obama said, “The friendship between the United States and Japan is extraordinarily important. It is for that reason that the prime minister is the first foreign dignitary to visit me in the Oval Office.”

Obama said the U.S.-Japanese alliance would be crucial to addressing international challenges, including climate change.

“We think we have to work together, not only on issues relating to the Pacific Rim, but throughout the world,” Obama added.

Aso said the global economy was also on the meeting’s agenda.

“We are the number 1 and second biggest economies of the world. We will have to work hand in hand. I think we are the only two nations which are powerful enough to solve those very critical, vital issue,” Aso said.

Japan’s Cabinet Secretary Takeo Kawamura said Aso’s status as the first foreign leader to visit the Obama White House indicated the priority the new president placed on the relationship.

Another topic likely to have been on the agenda was Japan’s Asian neighbor, North Korea, which U.S. intelligence says is preparing to test a long-range missile. Pyongyang has denied the allegation, saying instead that it is preparing to launch a satellite.

A North Korean test launch in 2006 failed 40 seconds after liftoff. The missile is thought to have an intended range of approximately 4,200 miles (6,700 kilometers), which—if accurate—could give it the capability to strike Alaska or Hawaii.

Aso’s visit to Washington comes as his approval rating stands at a meager 11 percent, the second-lowest ever recorded for a Japanese prime minister. Former Prime Minister Yoshiro Mori resigned after his rating fell to 9 percent.

Last week, Finance Minister Shoichi Nakagawa announced that he would step down after facing criticism for appearing intoxicated at a weekend news conference during the G-7 meeting in Rome.

CNN’s Chie Kobayashi contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — President Barack Obama held talks Tuesday with Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso, the first foreign leader welcomed by the new administration.

Aso arrived Monday at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland aboard his Boeing 747. His journey covered 6,800 miles (11,000 kilometers), although the meeting lasted only an hour and took place as Obama prepared to deliver his first speech before a joint session of Congress.

With Aso seated beside him at the White House, Obama emphasized the exceptional importance of the U.S.-Japan friendship. He said the strength of that relationship was why Aso became the first overseas dignitary to meet with him in the Oval Office.

According to Obama, cooperation between Washington and Tokyo would play a key role in addressing global challenges, including climate change. He added that the two countries needed to collaborate not just on Pacific Rim matters, but on issues worldwide.

Aso said the international economic situation was another subject discussed. Describing the United States and Japan as the world’s largest and second-largest economies, he said they must work closely together and suggested they were the only two nations with enough power to resolve such critical and essential problems.

Japan’s Cabinet Secretary, Takeo Kawamura, said Aso’s status as the Obama White House’s first foreign visitor demonstrated the high priority the new president gave to relations with Japan.

North Korea, Japan’s neighbor in Asia, was also expected to be among the topics discussed. U.S. intelligence officials say Pyongyang is getting ready to test a long-range missile. North Korea rejects that claim and says it is instead preparing to send a satellite into orbit.

A North Korean missile test in 2006 ended in failure 40 seconds after liftoff. The missile is believed to be designed for a range of roughly 4,200 miles (6,700 kilometers), potentially putting Alaska or Hawaii within reach.

Aso traveled to Washington while his public approval rating was only 11 percent, the second-lowest figure ever registered for a Japanese prime minister. Former Prime Minister Yoshiro Mori resigned after his rating fell to 9 percent.

The previous week, Finance Minister Shoichi Nakagawa said he would leave his post following criticism that he appeared drunk at a weekend news conference held during the G-7 gathering in Rome.

CNN’s Chie Kobayashi contributed to the report.

## Obama hosts Japan’s Aso in first White House meeting with foreign leader

**WASHINGTON —** President Barack Obama welcomed Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso to the White House on Tuesday, making Aso the first foreign leader hosted there since Obama took office.

The meeting underscored the importance of the U.S.-Japan alliance as both countries confront the global economic crisis, North Korea’s nuclear ambitions and the growing threat of climate change.

Obama described the alliance as a cornerstone of security in East Asia, while Aso emphasized Japan’s commitment to working closely with the new U.S. administration. The leaders discussed regional defense cooperation and the continued presence of American forces in Japan.

The economy dominated much of the talks, with the United States and Japan facing deep recessions following the global financial collapse. Both leaders called for coordinated international action to stabilize financial markets, support economic growth and resist protectionism ahead of upcoming global economic meetings.

Climate change was also on the agenda. Obama and Aso discussed efforts to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions, promote clean-energy technology and build international support for a new climate framework.

On North Korea, the leaders reaffirmed their commitment to the country’s denuclearization through diplomatic negotiations. They also addressed Pyongyang’s missile program and Japan’s concerns over Japanese citizens abducted by North Korean agents decades ago.

Aso’s visit was a relatively brief, business-focused meeting rather than a formal state occasion. Still, his selection as Obama’s first foreign guest at the White House sent a clear message about Washington’s commitment to its relationship with Tokyo.

The talks came as both leaders faced significant domestic economic and political pressures, adding urgency to their effort to demonstrate unity on some of the world’s most pressing challenges.

counterfactuals.output:
**Aso, Obama Reaffirm U.S.-Japan Alliance at White House**

**WASHINGTON, Feb. 24, 2009** — Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso met President Barack Obama at the White House on Tuesday, becoming the first foreign leader received there since Obama took office and underscoring the importance both governments placed on the U.S.-Japan alliance.

“The friendship between the United States and Japan is extraordinarily important to our two countries,” Obama said before the Oval Office talks. “It is the cornerstone of security in East Asia.”

Aso, speaking through an interpreter, said his early invitation demonstrated the value Washington placed on bilateral ties. “The fact that I am the very first guest here in the White House as a foreign leader is a testimony of the importance you attach to the Japan-U.S. alliance,” he said.

The leaders discussed the global financial crisis, North Korea’s nuclear program, Afghanistan and climate change. Their meeting came as both countries were struggling with severe economic contractions following the 2008 financial collapse. Japan’s export-dependent economy had fallen sharply, while the Obama administration was beginning to implement a major stimulus package and financial rescue measures.

Obama described Japan as a key partner in efforts to restore global growth and address regional security threats. The two leaders also reaffirmed plans to reorganize the U.S. military presence in Japan, including the relocation of thousands of Marines from Okinawa to Guam.

For Aso, the high-profile visit offered a diplomatic boost at a time of deep political weakness at home. His cabinet’s approval rating had fallen into the low teens in several Japanese polls, with some surveys putting support at or below 10 percent. Voters were increasingly dissatisfied with his handling of the recession, a series of verbal gaffes and divisions within his governing Liberal Democratic Party.

His standing had been further damaged days before the Washington trip by the resignation of Finance Minister Shoichi Nakagawa, who appeared drowsy and slurred his words at a news conference following a Group of Seven meeting in Rome. Nakagawa attributed his condition to cold medicine and alcohol, but the episode intensified criticism of Aso’s government.

Despite Aso’s domestic difficulties, Obama gave no public indication that Japan’s political uncertainty would diminish the alliance. He thanked the prime minister for making the trip and said the two nations would work closely on economic recovery and security.

The cordial meeting allowed Aso to present himself as a trusted partner of the new U.S. administration, but it remained unclear whether the symbolism of being Obama’s first foreign visitor could reverse his declining support in Japan ahead of elections due later in the year.

On February 24, 2009, President Barack Obama held a roughly one-hour Oval Office meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso—the first foreign leader received at the White House by the new administration. Obama had already traveled to Canada to meet Prime Minister Stephen Harper, but Aso’s invitation carried deliberate symbolic weight.

The two leaders focused on:

- Coordinating responses to the global financial crisis, with Japan then the world’s second-largest economy.
- Strengthening the U.S.–Japan security alliance and addressing North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs, as well as the abduction of Japanese citizens.
- Japanese support for stabilization and reconstruction in Afghanistan and Pakistan.
- Climate change, clean energy, trade, and preparations for upcoming international economic meetings.

Japan received the first White House visit principally to reassure Tokyo that the alliance remained a cornerstone of U.S. policy in Asia. Japanese officials had worried that Washington’s attention was shifting toward a rising China and that Japan might be taken for granted. By inviting Aso first—following Secretary of State Hillary Clinton’s decision to make Japan the first stop on her inaugural overseas trip—the administration signaled continuity, reliability, and Japan’s central role in regional security.

The choice also reflected practical needs. Amid a severe worldwide recession, Washington wanted close cooperation with a major economy, investor, creditor, and trading partner. Japan was also a longstanding host of U.S. forces and an important contributor to efforts in Afghanistan and elsewhere.

The reception itself was restrained, without the ceremony or major joint news conference associated with a state visit. That suggested the honor was intended less as a personal endorsement of Aso—whose approval ratings were poor—than as a strategic message about the importance of Japan and the bilateral alliance.

**Obama, Aso seek to reinforce U.S.-Japan alliance amid North Korea threat and political turmoil**

**WASHINGTON —** Japanese Prime Minister Taro Aso traveled roughly 6,800 miles from Tokyo to Washington for talks with President Barack Obama, a journey intended to reaffirm one of America’s most important Asian alliances at a moment of mounting security concerns abroad and deep political uncertainty in Japan.

Aso’s visit, early in the Obama administration, carried symbolic weight. He was the first foreign leader received by Obama at the White House, underscoring Washington’s desire to reassure Tokyo that the decades-old security partnership would remain central to U.S. policy in Asia even as the new president confronted wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and a rapidly worsening global economic crisis.

The meeting also came as North Korea appeared to be preparing a missile launch. Satellite observations and intelligence reports indicated activity at a North Korean launch facility, fueling suspicions that Pyongyang might test a long-range ballistic missile or launch a rocket it would describe as part of a civilian space program.

U.S. and Japanese officials viewed either possibility as a serious challenge. Japan lies within range of North Korea’s shorter-range missiles and has been especially sensitive to Pyongyang’s weapons programs since a North Korean rocket passed over Japanese territory in 1998. Tokyo has invested heavily in missile defenses developed with the United States, including sea-based interceptors and ground-based Patriot systems.

Obama and Aso were expected to emphasize close coordination with South Korea, China and Russia through the six-party negotiations aimed at ending North Korea’s nuclear program. The talks had produced agreements requiring Pyongyang to disable key nuclear facilities in exchange for economic and diplomatic benefits, but implementation had repeatedly stalled over verification and other disputes.

North Korea’s apparent launch preparations threatened to test the new U.S. administration’s approach. Obama had signaled a willingness to pursue direct diplomacy with adversaries, but officials also stressed that engagement would be accompanied by pressure and coordination with allies.

For Aso, the Washington trip offered an opportunity to demonstrate that Japan retained privileged access to the new American president. His government was struggling at home, where falling approval ratings, cabinet controversies and public anger over the economy had weakened the governing Liberal Democratic Party.

Japan had entered a severe recession as the global financial crisis battered exports, industrial production and employment. Aso’s efforts to respond with stimulus spending were complicated by political gridlock and criticism that his government lacked a clear strategy. Opposition parties, led by the Democratic Party of Japan, were pressing for an early general election and hoping to end the Liberal Democratic Party’s long dominance of postwar politics.

That domestic turmoil narrowed Aso’s room for maneuver. Although the alliance with Washington enjoyed broad institutional support, Japanese governments faced persistent disputes over the cost and location of U.S. bases, particularly on Okinawa, which hosts a large share of American forces stationed in Japan.

The Obama administration inherited plans to reorganize the U.S. military presence, including relocating thousands of Marines from Okinawa to Guam and replacing the crowded Marine Corps air station at Futenma. Both sides regarded the realignment as essential to sustaining the alliance, but implementation required money, local consent and political stability in Tokyo.

Economic policy was another major subject. The United States and Japan were the world’s two largest advanced economies, and both were under pressure to restore growth while resisting protectionism. Obama was advancing a large domestic recovery package, while Aso’s government had announced its own measures to support consumers and businesses.

Despite occasional trade friction, officials portrayed the relationship as extending well beyond bilateral commerce. Japan was a major contributor to international reconstruction efforts, provided logistical support for U.S.-led operations and remained a key partner on climate change, development assistance and nuclear nonproliferation.

The leaders were also expected to discuss Afghanistan and Pakistan, where Obama was reviewing American strategy. Japan had supplied fuel to coalition ships in the Indian Ocean and pledged substantial civilian aid, although constitutional limits and public resistance constrained the role of its armed forces overseas.

Aso’s 6,800-mile journey therefore served several purposes: reassuring a vulnerable ally, displaying unity in the face of North Korean pressure and giving an embattled Japanese prime minister a diplomatic success to present at home.

For Obama, the meeting was an early statement that closer engagement with China would not come at Japan’s expense. American officials have long sought to balance cooperation with Beijing against firm support for Tokyo, whose territory hosts tens of thousands of U.S. service members and provides the foundation for American military operations across the western Pacific.

The immediate results of the talks were likely to be measured less in new agreements than in tone. Both governments wanted to show that the alliance could adapt to a shifting regional order, a global financial emergency and political change in both countries.

Yet the challenges were already evident. North Korea’s suspected missile preparations threatened a new confrontation. Economic distress was intensifying pressure on both leaders. And Japan’s unstable domestic politics raised questions about how long Aso would remain in office and whether his successors would seek changes in the terms of the alliance.

For the moment, however, Washington and Tokyo presented a united front: the Obama administration affirming that Japan remained a cornerstone of U.S. strategy in Asia, and Aso arguing that close ties with the United States were indispensable to Japan’s security in an increasingly uncertain region.

Nakagawa stepped down after appearing disoriented at a news conference during a Group of Seven meeting in Rome, an episode that embarrassed Aso’s government as it sought to reassure investors about its handling of the economic crisis.

Climate change was also on the agenda, with both leaders considering ways to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and advance international negotiations toward a new global agreement. Japan, host of the 1997 Kyoto climate conference, had pressed major economies to cooperate on energy efficiency and clean technology.

On security, Obama and Aso reaffirmed the decades-old alliance between their countries and discussed North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs, regional stability and the continued presence of U.S. forces in Japan. The two governments also considered cooperation in Afghanistan and other international missions.

The White House said selecting Aso for Obama’s first meeting in Washington with a foreign leader reflected Japan’s central role in U.S. policy in Asia. The visit also offered Aso an opportunity to demonstrate the strength of the alliance as he faced low approval ratings and mounting pressure at home.
